15 Essential Post-Punk Albums
From the angular attack of Gang of Four to the gloomy sounds of the Cure, explore essential post-punk albums from the ’70s and ’80s.

images.alt: Essential post-punk records header image on Discogs featuring Joy Division

regions.text: Punk may have kicked down the door, but post-punk stepped through it and channeled the raw energy of its predecessor into something far more expansive. Emerging in the late 1970s, post-punk wasn’t defined by a single sound but by a shared desire to experiment, question, and rebuild. After co-founding the influential Buzzcocks in 1976, vocalist Howard Devoto left the band in early 1977, disillusioned by what he saw as the creative limitations of punk’s first wave. Later that year, he formed Magazine, a group that channeled the raw energy of punk into darker, more experimental terrain. With their 1977 debut, Pink Flag, Wire distilled punk into its most skeletal form, creating a minimalist framework that helped define the genre’s raw, no-frills ethos. Gang Of Four’s revolutionary debut, Entertainment!, released in 1979, remains one of post-punk’s most politically charged statements. The Pop Group’s Y arrived in 1979 like a Molotov cocktail hurled into the heart of post-punk. Drawing liberally from dub, free jazz, funk, and noise, the Bristol band paid no attention to genre boundaries. Devo’s Q: Are We Not Men? A: We Are Devo! reimagined punk through a lens of sci-fi satire and mechanical operation. Produced by Brian Eno and engineered by krautrock royalty Conny Plank, the album introduced the world to the band’s theory of de-evolution: the idea that instead of progressing, humanity was regressing.
